summary: Burning Activity Calendar is a free web app that joins more than two decades of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent calendar of burning activity. The MODIS record starts in 2000 and VIIRS in 2012, but VIIRS detects 2 to 5 times more fires, so the raw record jumps in 2012 and cannot be compared across years. We count fire-days on a 0.1° grid, fit a VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio for each month on the years both satellites observed, test it on held-out years, and use one VIIRS satellite at a time, scaling NOAA-20 to match S-NPP after S-NPP stopped. The result is one harmonized record from 2001 to today for eight Indian study areas (323 districts, 14 states). For any area, district or drawn rectangle, it shows a month-by-month calendar, the usual season and its critical periods, the next two weeks, season-timing trends, and districts burning far above usual, with an RSS alert feed. Early-warning teams, emergency responders, firefighters, land managers and scientists can see when and where to expect fire, and when this year is unusual.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Burning Activity Calendar turns NASA FIRMS active fire hotspots from MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP and NOAA-20) into one consistent burning calendar for any chosen area. It covers eight Indian study areas: Punjab & Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram & Manipur, Uttarakhand, Odisha & Chhattisgarh, Assam & neighbours, and Rajasthan. Together they hold 323 districts in 14 states, with up to 25 years of record.

You choose a study area, then pick a district from the list (or type its name), click one on the map, or drag a rectangle. The app then shows:

- The burning calendar: harmonized fire-days for every month since 2001 (2008 for the newer areas), as activity or against the usual level.

- This month and the next two weeks: the month so far against earlier years, what the coming 14 days usually bring, and how far the current season usually is by today.

- A typical year with its critical periods: the usual level and range for each day of the year, with this year drawn on top.

- Season timing: when 10%, 50% and 90% of each season's burning happened, with Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall trend tests.

- Burning more than usual: districts above 9 of 10 earlier years in the last 7, 14 or 30 days, outlined on the map, with a daily RSS feed and links to NASA FIRMS email alerts.

- Fires between two dates: any date range on the map, compared with the same dates in every other year.

- When India burns: every area's typical year on one calendar, ordered by peak, showing what is in season now and what starts next.

- Ask the calendar: plain questions such as "Is it unusual now?" or "Which districts?", answered from the same data as the charts. No AI is used.

- Compare two places, seven CSV downloads, a link that reopens the exact view, and a citation with the FIRMS product DOIs.

HOW IT WORKS (HARMONIZATION)

1. Clean: MODIS confidence 30 or above, VIIRS nominal or high, vegetation fires only, times converted to local dates.

2. Fire-days: a 0.1° grid cell counts once per day if it has any detection. This removes duplicates and much of the pixel-size difference (1 km MODIS against 375 m VIIRS).

3. One VIIRS satellite at a time, so adding satellites creates no jump. S-NPP stopped in November 2026. NOAA-20 counted 7-12% more fire-days over the 2026 overlap, so after the handover NOAA-20 is scaled down by 6-11%.

4. Calibrate: VIIRS ≈ k × MODIS, with one k for each calendar month, fitted on months both instruments observed. k ranges from 2.1 to 5.4 across the areas.

5. Convert: the MODIS-only years are scaled to VIIRS-equivalent.

6. Validate: leave-one-year-out error, and a jump test at the 2012 switch. In Punjab & Haryana, monthly k gives 14.1% held-out error against 21.1% for a single k, so we chose monthly k.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Fire managers get one record they can compare across 25 years, instead of two sensors that disagree. They can see when the critical period usually starts and peaks, whether this year is running above or below normal, and which districts need attention now. When we prepared the demo, 16 of Madhya Pradesh's 52 districts were burning far above usual and 4 were at a record. The app is aimed at early-warning teams, emergency responders, firefighters, land managers and scientists. It is free, needs no login, works on a phone, and any area can be added with three commands.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Data: NASA FIRMS API (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20 375 m), NASA Blue Marble imagery, geo Boundaries district boundaries.

- Processing: Python with pandas and numpy (download, cleaning, harmonization, validation, alerts).

- Website: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS; a 3D globe drawn directly in WebGL2 with NASA Blue Marble imagery; hand-built SVG and canvas charts; hosted free on GitHub Pages.

- Also: a Streamlit version (Plotly, Folium), automated tests that check the website's numbers match the Python results, and Git and GitHub.

- Hardware: ordinary laptops. No special hardware or paid services.

CREATIVITY

- A burning calendar, not just a fire map: time is the main axis, so a user immediately sees when burning happens and whether now is unusual.

- A 3D Earth with the four satellites in orbit opens the site. A scroll story then shows how the MODIS and VIIRS records are joined.

- "When India burns" puts every region's fire season on one national calendar, from Mizoram's jhum burning in March to Punjab's stubble burning in October and November.

- "Ask the calendar" answers plain questions without AI, so every answer can be traced to the data.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty: it is an activity index from satellite detections, not burned area and not an official warning. The page says so and lists what the record cannot tell you (cloud and smoke, small fires, overpass times).

- Consistency: no jumps at 2012, 2018, 2023 or the 2026 S-NPP handover.

- Usefulness: the questions fire managers ask (when, where, how unusual), plain language, and data downloads.

- Accessibility: mobile layout, keyboard use, and labels for screen readers on maps and charts.

- Openness: open NASA data, open code (MIT licence), and every number reproducible.

Use of AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped draft code and text following the team's instructions. The team chose the areas, design and method, and reviewed and tested everything. No AI-generated data is used; every number comes from NASA FIRMS.
